summary:
Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes stands under the French national framework. The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The region's own page carries no trans-specific content, and no regional deviation from the national position was identified.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees according to the sex inscribed on their identity documents, so trans women are held in men's facilities. BuzzFeed News reported on 12 January 2018 that transgender women incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal grey area and are punished for far more than their alleged crimes, drawing on first-person accounts including a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014 marked by detainee and staff hostility, and the incarceration of an Argentinian trans woman. The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty has stated that transgender detainees are the group that suffers the most in prison. The feature also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman held in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty, built on roughly forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections covering Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. It found persistent serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees, including placement by birth sex, isolation, exposure during strip searches, and overcrowding risks, and recommended that the 2016 depathologising law, which removed the surgery requirement for civil-status change, be translated into prison regulations. Its findings explicitly extend to intersex and non-binary detainees, and it identified structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees. Placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The legal baseline a trans visitor encounters is national. A bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017; it abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention. Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced the term sexual identity, itself protected since 2012.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013, with full adoption available; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect. Civil solidarity pacts have been available since 1999.
tangentialFactors:
France's anti-discrimination framework has carried gender identity and sexual orientation coverage in adjacent form for two decades. Penal Code article 225-1 protected sexual identity from 2012 before the term was replaced by gender identity in 2016, and a 31 December 2004 amendment set homophobic hate-speech penalties at up to EUR 45,000 and one year's imprisonment.

The 2021 custodial-inspection opinion rests on a decade of letters from detained trans people and on the authority's own findings that the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, that the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and that coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. The inspection programme behind it covered large men's and women's establishments and a central police station, indicating that the problems it identifies are not confined to a single facility type.

Discrimination reported to national oversight bodies is pervasive rather than exceptional: the Défenseur des droits frames its guidance around persistent violations confirmed from case files and association testimony, alongside a 2023 European survey in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination. Comparative reading of neighbouring jurisdictions is not sourced in this inventory.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in France proceeds by court application rather than medical intervention. The law of 18 November 2016, in force from 1 January 2017, abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements and rejected a Senate amendment demanding proof of medical treatment.

Gender-affirming treatment is funded through the national social-security system: transsexualism is classed under the long-term-illness category ALD 31.

Residents share the same partnership framework as visitors, with civil solidarity pacts available since 1999 and same-sex marriage with full adoption legal since 2013.

For residents held in custody, placement is decided by the sex on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, with each establishment improvising between special units and isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. The custodial-inspection authority recommended in 2021 that the 2016 depathologising law be written into prison regulations; that recommendation had not produced a marked change in placement practice by 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents the practice of border police, prison governorates or prefectures in Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes specifically. The national findings on detention and border questioning are assumed to apply, but no regional enforcement record, complaint or inspection visit for this region was located.

Whether the 2021 custodial-inspection recommendations have been implemented in regional places of detention, including any isolation practice in the region's men's and women's establishments, remains unresolved on the sources available.

Practical access for a short-stay visitor to gender-affirming care under ALD 31 is not sourced here; the funding arrangement described is a resident entitlement.

The Défenseur des droits framework decision on trans rights is cited for its findings and its guidance to service providers; its date, scope in law and any enforcement machinery it created are not established in this inventory.
